name: Paris
info: Paris is the capital of France, on the Seine. The Parisii settled there in the 3rd century BCE, the Romans founded Lutetia after 52 BCE, and it has been the French capital for most of the time since 508.

facts.founded: Settled by the Gallic Parisii between 250 and 225 BCE, with traces of earlier occupation from about 8000 BCE; the Romans built the town of Lutetia after their conquest of 52 BCE
facts.where: On the Seine, with the Île de la Cité at its heart, in the Île-de-France region of northern France
facts.known: the Parisii and Roman Lutetia; Notre-Dame and the Gothic style; the University of Paris; the French Revolution; Haussmann's rebuilding; the siege and Commune of 1870–71; the occupation of 1940–44; its museums and artists
facts.today: Paris is the capital and largest city of France, where the president and both houses of Parliament sit.

t: Paris began as a settlement of the Gallic Parisii on the Seine, became the Roman town of Lutetia after 52 BCE, and was made capital by Clovis I in 508.

The Capetian kings built it up from the 12th century into the political, religious and learning centre of France, with Notre-Dame, the Louvre and the University, and in 1328 it was the most populous city in Europe.
From the Revolution of 1789 through Haussmann's rebuilding, the siege and Commune of 1870–71 and the occupation of 1940–44, Paris was repeatedly the scene of upheaval and violence.
dyk: In September 1914, about 600 Paris taxis carried 6,000 soldiers to the front at the First Battle of the Marne, each taking five men, and the task was done within twenty-four hours.
ev: The Parisii are defeated by a Roman army under Titus Labienus, and the Romans build Lutetia
Clovis I makes Paris his capital
Construction of the cathedral of Notre-Dame begins
The plague of 1348–1349 kills forty to fifty thousand Parisians, a quarter of the population
The St Bartholomew's Day massacre kills about three thousand Protestants in Paris
A crowd storms the Bastille on 14 July and Paris becomes the stage of the Revolution
The Commune is crushed in the Bloody Week
The city is liberated on 25 August after four years of German occupation

sections.origins:
The oldest traces of human occupation in Paris date from about 8000 BCE, in the Mesolithic period: archaeologists digging in the 15th arrondissement in 2008 found remains of a hunter-gatherer settlement. At Bercy, excavations in 1991 found fragments of three wooden canoes used by fishermen on the Seine, the oldest dated to 4800–4300 BCE, and Neolithic hatchets made in eastern Europe, which show that the first Parisians already traded with other parts of Europe.

Between 250 and 225 BCE the Parisii, a Gallic tribe, settled on the banks of the Seine. One of the area's main north–south trade routes crossed the river on the Île de la Cité, and the Parisii traded with river towns as far away as the Iberian Peninsula and minted their own coins. They built an oppidum, a walled fort, at the beginning of the 2nd century BCE, but its site is disputed. It may have stood on the Île de la Cité, where Julius Caesar recorded meeting the leaders of the Parisii on an island in the Seine. Other historians point to the absence of early Gallic traces there and place it at Nanterre, where the remains of a large settlement were found in the 1980s. Strabo called the settlement Lucotocia and Ptolemy Leucotecia. The meaning of the tribal name is debated: one proposal derives it from a Celtic root for 'cauldron'.
sections.growth:
After the Roman conquest the city lay mostly on the Left Bank, around a forum on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève. It had an aqueduct sixteen kilometres long, baths and an amphitheatre for ten to fifteen thousand spectators, although its population was only six to eight thousand. It remained a medium-sized city, much smaller than Lugdunum (Lyon) or Agedincum (Sens).

In the 12th century the Capetian kings, who held little more than Paris and its surroundings, built it up as the political, economic, religious and cultural capital of France. Work on Notre-Dame began in 1163, Suger rebuilt the basilica of Saint-Denis in the style later called Gothic, and Philip II built the Louvre fortress, new walls, stone bridges and the covered market of Les Halles. In 1328 the population was about 200,000, the largest of any city in Europe. It reached 250,000 by 1500 and 400,000 in 1643, and was between 600,000 and 640,000 in 1789. Rebuilding from 1853 took it past a million, and its historic peak was 2.9 million in 1921. In the 16th century Paris printed more books than any other European city, and by the mid-19th century it was a financial centre second only to London.
sections.rulers:
The Romans held Paris from 52 BCE. From 355 to 360 it was the base of Julian, the Caesar of the western provinces, whose soldiers proclaimed him Augustus in February 360, and Valentinian I and Gratian also wintered there. Clovis I, King of the Franks, entered the city in 486 and made it his capital in 508. The Carolingians, in power from 751, moved the Frankish capital to Aachen, and Paris regained its place under the Capetians, a dynasty founded by Hugh Capet in 987.

During the Hundred Years' War an Anglo-Burgundian army took the city on 28 May 1418, Henry V of England held it from 1420, and the infant Henry VI was crowned king of France there in 1431. Charles VII returned in 1436. Francis I made the Louvre his residence in 1534. After the Fronde, Louis XIV moved the court to Versailles (in 1671 by one account, in 1682 by another), and the regent returned the government to Paris in 1715 before it went back to Versailles in 1722.

The Revolution gave Paris its first independent city council on 15 July 1789. Napoleon replaced the elected mayor with a prefect of the Seine in 1800, and prefects governed the city until Jacques Chirac became its first elected mayor since the Revolution on 25 March 1977. Napoleon III annexed the surrounding towns in 1860, and the Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris on 4 September 1870.
sections.life:
In Roman Lutetia excavations have found amphorae of Italian wine and olive oil, shellfish and the remains of garum. Christianity arrived in the middle of the 3rd century; according to tradition it was brought by Saint Denis, the first bishop, who was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre. The first recognised bishop, Victorinus, is dated to 346, and by 392 the city had a cathedral.

Medieval Paris divided by function. The Île de la Cité held the royal palace and the cathedral, the Left Bank the schools and monasteries, and the Right Bank the port, the market and the merchants, whose league, the Hanse parisienne, became a powerful force. The Left Bank was called the Latin Quarter because Latin was the language of teaching; some twenty thousand students lived there, and the teachers included Pierre Abelard, Thomas Aquinas, Roger Bacon and Bonaventure. Robert de Sorbon opened the college later named the Sorbonne in 1257. Saint Louis created the Provost of the Merchants and the first municipal council, of twenty-four members.

By the 1720s there were around 400 cafés, where writers and scholars met, and Diderot and d'Alembert published the Encyclopédie in 1751–52. Daniel Roche estimated that in 1700 between 150,000 and 200,000 people received poor relief, about a third of the population. In the 19th century large factories were built on the edges of the city, while the centre kept its artisans making clothing, watches, furniture, porcelain and leather goods.
sections.crises:
In December 856 Vikings burned Paris, sparing a few churches for a ransom. Their siege of 885–886 failed against the Seine and the walls of the Île de la Cité. The plague of 1348–1349 killed forty to fifty thousand Parisians, a quarter of the population, and there were at least 36 occasions of plague in the city between 1348 and 1480. In the Hundred Years' War the city was occupied, and when the English left in 1436 many areas lay in ruins and 100,000 inhabitants, half the population, had gone.

On the night of 23–24 August 1572 the royal council decided to kill the Protestant leaders then in Paris for the wedding of Henry of Navarre, and Catholic mobs turned it into a general slaughter. About three thousand Protestants were killed in Paris and five to ten thousand elsewhere in France. In the Revolution, bands broke into the prisons in September 1792 and murdered priests, aristocrats and criminals. In the Terror, 16,594 people were tried by the revolutionary tribunal and guillotined.

The Prussian siege from 19 September 1870 brought cold and hunger, so that even the zoo's elephants were killed for food, and the city surrendered on 28 January 1871. The Commune that followed was retaken in the 'Bloody Week' of 21–28 May. Nearly 7,000 Communards were killed in combat or shot afterwards, and about 10,000 were sentenced to prison or deportation. On 16–17 July 1942 the French police arrested 12,884 Jews on German orders, and most were sent to Auschwitz.
sections.legacy:
Haussmann's rebuilding gave central Paris the street plan and the look it still has: buildings of the same height and design, faced in creamy white stone, along wide boulevards, with four large new parks and new sewers and water mains. The city was in turn the birthplace of Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism, the home of writers and artists of the 1920s in Montparnasse, and the setting of the intellectual life of Saint-Germain-des-Prés after 1945. The first public projection of a motion picture was given at the Grand Café on 25 December 1895.

Paris is nicknamed the 'City of Light', which is attributed mainly to its leading role in the Age of Enlightenment. The Eiffel Tower, built for the Exposition of 1889, was denounced at first in public letters by prominent cultural figures. Parts of the city along the Seine have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The fire of 15 April 2019 destroyed the spire and most of the roof of Notre-Dame, and the cathedral reopened on 7 December 2024.

Paris is today the capital and largest city of France, with about two million inhabitants, fewer than its peak of 2.9 million in 1921, and the seat of the president and both houses of Parliament. Its metropolitan area has more than thirteen million people.

summary: Paris grew from a settlement of the Gallic Parisii on the Seine into the Roman town of Lutetia and, from 508, the capital of the Frankish kings and later of France. It was a centre of learning, the stage of the Revolution and the city remade by Haussmann.
notes: start -250 (circa) is the Parisii settlement (250-225 BCE; paris.txt: around the middle of the 3rd century BCE). Traces of human occupation go back to about 8000 BCE; I used the city's settlement, not the Mesolithic find.
Disagreement: peak population. History of Paris intro says 2.1 million in 1921; its Great Depression section and the Paris article say 2.9 million in 1921. I used 2.9 million.
Disagreement: Vikings. Paris article: sacking by Vikings in 845; History of Paris: 'December 856' (845 not mentioned). I used 856 only.
Disagreement: Louis XIV's move to Versailles, 1671 (history) vs 1682 (Paris article); both given in the text.
Disagreement: Terror toll, 16,594 tried and guillotined (history, apparently in Paris) vs 'more than 16,000 others throughout France' (Paris article). Both given.

Disagreement (not used): children in the Vel d'Hiv roundup, 4,051 (history) vs 4,115 (Paris article); I gave only the 12,884 total, which both agree on. Commune's start: history says power taken 26 March, Paris article 28 March; left out.

Disagreement (not used): the University of Paris was 'originally organised in the mid-12th century' (history, also 'mid-13th century' in its lead) vs founded 1190 by Philip II (Paris article); I gave neither date. The Sorbonne's opening in 1257 is from the history.
Population 1789: 600,000 to 640,000 (history) vs 650,000 in 1780 (Paris article); I used the 1789 range only. 1640: about 400,000 in both.

Clovis: history says he entered Paris in 486 and, by being interred there, gave it weight; 508 as capital is from the Paris article and the history's lead. The history gives 511 for the division of the kingdom, left out.

Left out: Louis XIV and later periods' architecture in detail, the Belle Epoque expositions' figures, 1961 and 1968 events, 2015 attacks, 2024 Olympics, as space did not allow; and the Paris article's 'City of Light' is given only as the article's own attribution. The 15 April 2019 fire and 7 December 2024 reopening are from the Paris article.

Wanted but not found: any figure for the dead of the 1572 massacre beyond 'about three thousand' in Paris; a total for people deported in 1942 or survivors; the number of Parisians killed in the Revolution's September massacres 1792 (the history gives no figure); the 1870-71 siege death toll.
